summary: Defines a Content-ID access method for the MIME Message/External-Body type, letting an external body refer to an object by the Content-ID of another part of the message. It is experimental.

eli5.summary: Instead of copying a thing into a note, the note points to where it can already be found.

questions: what is the content-id access type
how does message/external-body refer to objects
subtitle: A MIME access type that lets one message part point to another part of the same message instead of repeating its data.

tldr.problem: A MIME message holding a structured object may contain the same element several times, and copying the data into each body part wastes bandwidth and storage.
tldr.mechanism: A Message/External-Body part with access-type content-id carries a Content-ID header that matches another body part in the same message, and the mail reader builds the full part from the two.
tldr.outcome: Duplicated data is sent once while the structure of the object is kept. The type is experimental.

today: RFC 1873 is an Experimental protocol, not an Internet standard, and the unit metadata shows no later RFC replacing it.

sections.title: Why Refer Within a Message
sections.content:
When MIME is used to wrap a structured object with many elements, such as an SGML document, one element may occur several times. Each element normally maps to a MIME entity, but it is useful to include repeated elements exactly once while keeping the object structure.

Consider a multipart entity where several body parts contain the same data but different parameters or Content-* headers. Not duplicating the data in each saves bandwidth and storage space. The existing Message/External-Body type points to objects outside the message; this access type points to an object inside it.
sections.eli5: If the same picture appears many times, send it once and let the other spots point to it.

sections.title: The content-id Access Type
sections.content:
The access-type name is content-id, with no required or optional parameters. The Content-ID header of the referring part must match exactly one Content-ID in the same message, not counting other content-id access-type entities. So the type can only occur inside a multipart message, and it may refer to a body part anywhere in that message.

The mail user agent builds the result from five pieces: the referenced part's content-type header, the referring part's other headers, any headers of the referenced part that the referring part lacks, the blank line that ends the headers, and the referenced part's body.
sections.eli5: The reader glues the note and the thing it points to together into one finished piece.

sections.title: Example
sections.content:
The RFC shows a Multipart/Mixed message with two identical images. The first part is an image/jpeg with a Content-ID. The second is a Message/External-Body part with access-type=content-id and the same Content-ID, and no body of its own.

After the reader resolves it, the second part becomes an image/jpeg with the same data and the second part's own Content-Description, which reads that the body part is duplicated by reference.
sections.eli5: The second picture is just a sticky note saying 'same as the first one', and the reader swaps in the real picture.

sections.title: Security Notes
sections.content: The RFC says the content-id access type does not affect the security of messages or systems. It adds that the referenced MIME entity may have security implications of its own.
sections.eli5: The pointer itself is harmless, but what it points to still needs the usual care.

data.title: Two identical images
data.code:
MIME-Version: 1.0
Content-Type: Multipart/Mixed;
   boundary=tiger-lily

--tiger-lily
Content-Type: image/jpeg
Content-ID: <950323.1552@XIson.com>

AAAcdb...
--tiger-lily
Content-type: Message/External-Body;
   access-type=content-id
Content-ID: <950323.1552@XIson.com>
Content-Description:
   This body part is duplicated by reference

--tiger-lily--

references.text: Crocker, D., "Standard for the Format of ARPA Internet Text Messages", STD 11, RFC 822, UDEL, August 1982.
Borenstein, N., and N. Freed, "MIME (Multipurpose Internet Mail Extensions) Part One", RFC 1521, Bellcore, Innosoft, September 1993.
